meta.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
meta.author: bank-team-psychology
meta.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Identify the part of a neuron that receives incoming signals
questions.stem: In a train dispatcher's log, which neuronal part is recorded as the receiver of incoming signals from other cells?

options.text: The dendrite receives signals and passes them toward the cell body
The axon carries signals away toward the next cell in the circuit
options.misconception: confuses the output fibre with the input region

options.text: The soma generates the action potential all on its own
options.misconception: overstates the cell body's sole role in triggering

options.text: The terminal button releases transmitter into the cleft
options.misconception: confuses the release site with the reception site

questions.explanation: Dendrites are the input structures that receive signals from other neurons. The axon, soma and terminal have different roles, so choosing them mixes up the direction of information flow.
questions.hint: Look for the input branch of the cell.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a speed measurement for neural conduction
questions.stem: A log entry states a myelinated fibre conducts at 120 metres per second. What is that speed in kilometres per hour?
questions.explanation: Multiplying 120 metres per second by 3.6 gives 432 kilometres per hour. A common slip is to divide by 3.6 instead, which would give 33.3.

questions.learningObjective: Match a neurotransmitter to its functional role
questions.stem: A diagram of a synapse shows a molecule that slows neural activity and promotes calm. Which molecule is labelled?

options.text: Glutamate, the main excitatory messenger in the brain
Dopamine, linked to reward and movement pathways
options.misconception: confuses a modulator with the main inhibitor

options.text: GABA, the main inhibitory messenger in the brain
Acetylcholine, involved in muscle activation and memory
options.misconception: confuses a cholinergic role with inhibition

questions.explanation: GABA is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter and reduces neural firing. Glutamate is excitatory, while dopamine and acetylcholine have other primary roles.
questions.hint: Think of the main brake pedal of the brain.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a region is tied to a function
questions.stem: Why does damage to the hippocampus disrupt the formation of new long-term memories?

answer.exemplar: The hippocampus consolidates new declarative memories into lasting storage, so damage interrupts that consolidation while older memories remain largely intact.

questions.explanation: The hippocampus binds and consolidates new episodic and semantic memories. Damage leaves earlier memories mostly intact but blocks new lasting traces from forming.
questions.hint: Focus on consolidation of new traces.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an agonist from an antagonist
questions.stem: A substance mimics a neurotransmitter and activates its receptor. What is this called?

options.text: An antagonist blocks the receptor and prevents activation
An enzyme deactivator stops breakdown of the transmitter
options.misconception: confuses metabolic block with receptor activation

options.text: A reuptake inhibitor prolongs transmitter in the cleft
options.misconception: confuses reuptake block with direct activation

options.text: An agonist mimics the transmitter and activates the receptor

questions.explanation: An agonist mimics the natural transmitter and turns the receptor on. An antagonist blocks it, and reuptake or enzyme effects work indirectly.
questions.hint: Agonist means it turns the switch on.

questions.learningObjective: Order the steps of synaptic transmission
questions.stem: In a log, calcium influx occurs before vesicle fusion. What event must follow vesicle fusion at the synapse?
questions.explanation: After vesicle fusion the transmitter is released into the cleft, which is the next step counted as one event. Confusing release with reuptake would add an extra step.

questions.stem: A graph of membrane voltage shows a spike that either reaches full size or does not occur. What principle does this illustrate?

options.text: The all-or-none principle governs action potentials
Graded potentials grow in proportion to stimulus strength
Frequency coding changes the amplitude of each spike
options.misconception: confuses rate with size of spikes

options.text: The refractory period lengthens the spike duration

questions.explanation: Action potentials are all-or-none: once threshold is reached the spike is full size. Graded potentials vary with stimulus strength instead.
questions.hint: The spike size does not scale with stimulus.

questions.learningObjective: Map a lobe to its primary function
questions.stem: Which cortical lobe is primarily responsible for processing visual information?

answer.exemplar: The occipital lobe at the back of the cortex is the primary visual processing area, handling incoming visual signals from the eyes.

questions.explanation: The occipital lobe is the primary visual cortex. Other lobes handle sound, touch, or planning instead.
questions.hint: Think of the lobe at the rear of the head.

questions.stem: Language production is most commonly lateralized to which hemisphere in most people?

options.text: Both hemispheres share language equally in everyone
The right hemisphere dominates language in most people
The left hemisphere dominates language in most people
Language has no hemispheric bias at all

questions.explanation: In most individuals the left hemisphere is dominant for language production. The right hemisphere handles other tasks like spatial attention.
questions.hint: The dominant side for speech in most people.

questions.learningObjective: Name a limbic structure and its role
questions.stem: A log lists the amygdala as active during a fear response. How many primary limbic structures are commonly grouped with it in basic accounts?
questions.explanation: Basic accounts group the amygdala with the hippocampus, hypothalamus and thalamus as key limbic structures. Counting only three would omit one of these.
questions.hint: Count amygdala plus three close partners.

questions.learningObjective: Link a memory type to its neural substrate
questions.stem: A brain diagram highlights the cerebellum. Which kind of memory is most associated with this structure?

options.text: Working memory holding items briefly
options.misconception: confuses short-term with long-term skill memory

options.text: Episodic autobiographical memory
Semantic factual knowledge
options.misconception: confuses fact memory with skill memory

options.text: Procedural and motor skill memory

questions.explanation: The cerebellum supports procedural and motor skill memory. Declarative and working memory rely more on cortical and hippocampal circuits.

questions.learningObjective: Explain a behaviour from a neural cause
questions.stem: How can a lesion in the frontal lobe change a person's decision-making and impulse control?

answer.exemplar: The frontal lobe houses executive functions that inhibit impulses and weigh consequences, so damage weakens control and leads to risky or socially inappropriate choices.

questions.explanation: Frontal regions implement executive control and inhibition. Damage reduces the ability to weigh consequences and suppress impulses.

questions.learningObjective: Connect a sleep stage to brain activity
questions.stem: During which sleep stage does the brain show rapid eye movement and vivid dreaming?

options.text: Stage three is when most dreaming vividly occurs
options.misconception: confuses slow-wave sleep with REM dreaming

options.text: Stage one is the deepest restorative sleep stage
options.misconception: confuses light sleep with deep restoration

options.text: REM sleep is marked by rapid eye movement and dreaming
Wakefulness is when eye movements are fastest
options.misconception: confuses waking with the REM stage

questions.explanation: REM sleep is defined by rapid eye movement and vivid dreams. Slow-wave sleep is deeper and less dream-rich.
questions.hint: The stage named for eye movement.

questions.stem: Twin data show identical twins raised apart are more alike than fraternal twins raised together. What does this suggest?
questions.explanation: The pattern suggests a strong genetic contribution, counted as two influences favouring nature over shared environment. Treating it as one factor would understate the evidence.
questions.hint: Count the two pieces favouring genetics.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish axon from dendrite by direction
questions.stem: A diagram labels the structure that sends signals away from the cell body. Which label is correct?

options.text: Dendrite carries signals toward the cell body
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the axon

options.text: Myelin generates the electrical impulse itself
Soma carries signals to neighbouring cells
options.misconception: confuses the cell body with the output fibre

options.text: Axon carries signals away from the cell body

questions.explanation: The axon is the output fibre carrying signals away. Dendrites bring signals in, and myelin only insulates.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of myelin on speed
questions.stem: Why does a myelinated axon conduct impulses faster than an unmyelinated one?

answer.exemplar: Myelin insulates the axon and forces the impulse to jump between nodes of Ranvier, which speeds conduction while saving energy.

questions.explanation: Myelin insulates and permits saltatory conduction between nodes. This raises speed and reduces energy use compared with continuous conduction.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a catecholamine neurotransmitter involved in reward and movement?

options.text: Serotonin regulates mood and sleep cycles
options.misconception: confuses an indolamine with a catecholamine

options.text: GABA is the main inhibitory amino acid transmitter
options.misconception: confuses an amino acid with a catecholamine

options.text: Dopamine is a catecholamine tied to reward and movement
Acetylcholine is a cholinergic messenger at muscles
options.misconception: confuses a cholinergic with a catecholamine

questions.explanation: Dopamine is a catecholamine linked to reward and movement. Serotonin, GABA and acetylcholine belong to other chemical classes.
questions.hint: Reward and movement point to one messenger.

questions.stem: A log shows the thalamus relays 90 percent of sensory input to the cortex. What percentage bypasses it?
questions.explanation: If 90 percent is relayed, then 100 minus 90 equals 10 percent bypasses the thalamus. The olfactory route is a known exception.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a reuptake inhibitor works
questions.stem: A diagram shows a drug blocking the transporter that returns serotonin to the presynaptic neuron. What is the drug?

options.text: An enzyme inhibitor stops breakdown of the transmitter
options.misconception: confuses metabolic block with reuptake block

options.text: An antagonist blocks the postsynaptic receptor directly
options.misconception: confuses transporter block with receptor block

options.text: An agonist mimics serotonin and activates the receptor
A reuptake inhibitor keeps serotonin in the cleft longer

questions.explanation: Blocking the reuptake transporter leaves more serotonin in the synaptic cleft. This differs from antagonism, agonism or enzyme inhibition.
questions.hint: The target is the transporter, not the receptor.

questions.learningObjective: Explain vesicle release dependence on calcium
questions.stem: Why does blocking calcium channels at the terminal prevent neurotransmitter release?

answer.exemplar: Calcium entry triggers vesicle fusion with the membrane, so without calcium the vesicles cannot release their transmitter into the cleft.

questions.explanation: Calcium influx is the trigger for vesicle fusion. Without it the transmitter stays stored and no signal crosses the cleft.
questions.hint: Calcium is the trigger for fusion.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the ion that drives depolarization
questions.stem: Which ion rushing into the neuron causes the rising phase of the action potential?

options.text: Calcium influx drives the rising phase of the spike
Potassium influx drives the rising phase of the spike
options.misconception: reverses the roles of sodium and potassium

options.text: Sodium influx drives the rising phase of the spike
Chloride influx drives the rising phase of the spike
options.misconception: confuses an inhibitory ion with excitation

questions.explanation: Sodium rushing in depolarizes the membrane. Potassium leaves during repolarization, and calcium or chloride play other roles.
questions.hint: The ion that makes the cell more positive.

questions.stem: A log notes that two of the four cortical lobes are mainly sensory. How many are not primarily sensory?
questions.explanation: With four lobes total and two mainly sensory, the remaining two are not primarily sensory. Frontal and temporal handle other functions.
questions.hint: Subtract the sensory lobes from four.

questions.stem: A diagram shows an object presented to the left visual field reaching the right hemisphere. What can the person verbally report?

options.text: The person can name the object because the left hemisphere saw it
options.misconception: ignores which hemisphere received the input

options.text: The person sees nothing at all in that field
options.misconception: confuses lack of report with lack of perception

options.text: The person can write the name with the left hand only
options.misconception: confuses motor output with verbal report

options.text: The person often cannot name the object verbally

questions.explanation: The right hemisphere perceives the object but lacks direct speech control, so verbal naming is often impaired. Perception itself is intact.

questions.stem: Why is the hypothalamus considered a bridge between the nervous and endocrine systems?

answer.exemplar: The hypothalamus receives neural input and controls the pituitary gland, translating nervous signals into hormonal release throughout the body.

questions.explanation: The hypothalamus links neural activity to pituitary hormone release. This bridges fast nervous signals with slower hormonal effects.

questions.stem: Approximately how many items can be held in short-term memory at once?

options.text: About two items regardless of chunking
About seventy items in short-term store
About seven plus or minus two items
About unlimited items with rehearsal

questions.explanation: Short-term memory holds roughly seven plus or minus two items. Chunking can raise the effective amount but not the raw slot count.

questions.stem: A log shows dopamine levels at 60 percent of baseline in a patient with movement problems. What percentage was lost?
questions.explanation: If levels are at 60 percent of baseline, then 100 minus 60 equals 40 percent was lost. This mirrors the dopamine loss seen in Parkinson's disease.
questions.hint: Subtract the remaining level from one hundred.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why sleep supports brain function
questions.stem: A diagram labels sleep as a period when the brain clears metabolic waste. Which process is highlighted?

options.text: Neurogenesis peaks only during deep wakefulness
Synaptic pruning only happens while awake
Myelination stops entirely during sleep
Glymphatic clearance removes waste during sleep

questions.explanation: The glymphatic system clears metabolic waste during sleep. Other processes like pruning or myelination follow different schedules.

questions.stem: Why does a genetic predisposition for anxiety often require a stressful environment to appear?

answer.exemplar: Genes can raise vulnerability while environmental stress activates the pathway, so the trait emerges only when both factors combine.

questions.explanation: Genetic vulnerability sets a threshold and environmental stress can cross it. Neither alone is usually sufficient.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the protective sheath of an axon
questions.stem: What is the fatty sheath that insulates many axons and speeds conduction?

options.text: Dendrite is the fatty sheath around the cell body
options.misconception: confuses an input branch with insulation

options.text: Myelin is the fatty insulating sheath around axons
Synapse is the fatty covering of the axon
options.misconception: confuses a junction with a sheath

options.text: Soma is the fatty layer around nerve fibres
options.misconception: confuses the cell body with insulation

questions.explanation: Myelin is the fatty sheath. Dendrites, synapses and soma are not insulating layers.
questions.hint: The fatty wrapper around the fibre.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate conduction time over a distance
questions.stem: An impulse travels 6 metres at 30 metres per second. How many milliseconds does it take?
questions.explanation: Time equals distance divided by speed, so 6 divided by 30 equals 0.2 seconds, which is 200 milliseconds. Forgetting to convert to milliseconds gives 0.2.

questions.stem: A diagram links a transmitter to mood regulation and sleep. Which transmitter is shown?

options.text: GABA mainly inhibits neural firing broadly
Dopamine mainly regulates reward and movement
Serotonin regulates mood and sleep-wake cycles
Acetylcholine mainly activates muscles and memory

questions.explanation: Serotonin is tied to mood and sleep-wake cycles. Dopamine, GABA and acetylcholine have different primary roles.
questions.hint: Mood and sleep point to one messenger.

questions.stem: Why does damage to the parietal lobe often produce neglect of one side of space?

answer.exemplar: The parietal lobe integrates spatial attention, so damage disrupts awareness of the opposite side of space even though vision itself remains intact.

questions.explanation: Parietal regions direct spatial attention. Damage can make a person ignore one side despite intact sensory pathways.

questions.learningObjective: Classify a drug by its effect on a receptor
questions.stem: A drug sits on a receptor but does not activate it, blocking the natural transmitter. What is it?

options.text: An enzyme inhibitor slows transmitter breakdown
An agonist activates the receptor like the transmitter
A reuptake inhibitor blocks the transporter protein
An antagonist occupies the receptor without activating it

questions.explanation: An antagonist binds without activating and blocks the natural transmitter. Agonists, reuptake inhibitors and enzyme inhibitors act differently.

questions.stem: A log records a synaptic delay of 0.5 milliseconds. How many such delays fit in one millisecond?
questions.explanation: One millisecond divided by 0.5 milliseconds equals 2 delays. A common error is to multiply instead of divide.

questions.stem: A voltage trace shows a brief period after a spike when no new spike can fire. What is this called?

options.text: The resting potential is the brief no-fire interval
The refractory period limits how fast a neuron fires
The threshold is the period of no firing
The synaptic delay is the no-fire interval

questions.explanation: The refractory period is the recovery interval that caps firing rate. It is not the resting potential, threshold or synaptic delay.
questions.hint: The recovery window after a spike.

questions.stem: Why does damage to the temporal lobe often impair language comprehension?

answer.exemplar: The temporal lobe contains areas that decode spoken and written language, so damage disrupts comprehension even when hearing remains intact.

questions.explanation: Temporal regions decode language meaning. Damage can leave hearing intact while comprehension suffers.

questions.stem: What structure connects the two cerebral hemispheres and allows them to share information?

options.text: The brainstem connects the two hemispheres
options.misconception: confuses a lower centre with the bridge

options.text: The thalamus connects the two hemispheres directly
options.misconception: confuses a relay with an interhemispheric bridge

options.text: The corpus callosum links the two hemispheres
The cerebellum connects the two hemispheres

questions.explanation: The corpus callosum is the main interhemispheric bridge. The thalamus, brainstem and cerebellum serve other functions.

questions.stem: A log shows amygdala activation 3 times baseline during a threat. If baseline is 5 units, what is activation?
questions.explanation: Three times a baseline of 5 units gives 15 units. Multiplying baseline by the factor gives the activation level.

questions.stem: A diagram shows a patient who cannot form new memories after an injury but recalls old ones. What condition is shown?

options.text: Semantic dementia erases factual knowledge only
Retrograde amnesia erases old memories before injury
options.misconception: reverses the time direction of loss

options.text: Working memory loss removes all brief storage
options.misconception: confuses a store with a consolidation failure

options.text: Anterograde amnesia blocks new memory formation

questions.explanation: Anterograde amnesia impairs forming new memories after injury while older memories remain. Retrograde loss affects pre-injury memories instead.
questions.hint: New memories after the injury are lost.

questions.stem: Why does loss of dopamine-producing neurons lead to movement difficulties?

answer.exemplar: Dopamine in the basal ganglia helps initiate and smooth movement, so neuron loss produces tremor, rigidity and slowness.

questions.explanation: Dopamine supports movement initiation and smoothing. Its loss produces the motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease.

questions.stem: Which disorder involves repeated pauses in breathing during sleep?

options.text: Narcolepsy involves sudden sleep attacks
options.misconception: confuses a breathing disorder with sleep attacks

options.text: Sleep apnoea involves repeated breathing pauses
Insomnia involves difficulty falling asleep
options.misconception: confuses a breathing disorder with insomnia

options.text: Somnambulism involves walking while asleep
options.misconception: confuses a breathing disorder with sleepwalking

questions.explanation: Sleep apnoea is defined by repeated breathing pauses. Narcolepsy, insomnia and sleepwalking are different conditions.

questions.stem: A log cites a heritability of 0.60 for a trait. What percentage of variance is attributed to genetic differences?
questions.explanation: A heritability of 0.60 corresponds to 60 percent of variance attributed to genetic differences. Multiplying by 100 converts the proportion.
questions.hint: Multiply the proportion by one hundred.

questions.stem: A diagram shows branching fibres that collect input from many other neurons. What are they?

options.text: Terminals collect signals from the cleft
Axons collect input from other cells
Dendrites collect and combine incoming signals
Myelin collects electrical charge

questions.explanation: Dendrites are the branching input collectors. Axons, terminals and myelin serve other roles.

questions.stem: Why is conduction in a myelinated axon called saltatory?

answer.exemplar: The impulse jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next instead of travelling continuously, which is what saltatory means.

questions.explanation: Saltatory means leaping. The impulse jumps between nodes of Ranvier rather than moving continuously along the membrane.

questions.stem: Which amino acid is the brain's main excitatory neurotransmitter?

options.text: Taurine is the main excitatory amino acid
options.misconception: confuses a modulator with the main excitatory transmitter

options.text: GABA is the main excitatory amino acid
Glycine is the main excitatory amino acid
options.misconception: confuses an inhibitory amino acid with excitation

options.text: Glutamate is the main excitatory amino acid

questions.explanation: Glutamate is the principal excitatory amino acid. GABA and glycine are inhibitory, and taurine is not the main excitatory messenger.

questions.learningObjective: Map a region to its motor role
questions.stem: A log records the motor cortex in the frontal lobe controlling voluntary movement. How many hemispheres contain a motor cortex?
questions.explanation: Each cerebral hemisphere has its own motor cortex, so there are two. Counting one would ignore bilateral organisation.

questions.stem: A diagram shows a drug's effect weakening after repeated doses. What phenomenon is illustrated?

options.text: Withdrawal occurs while the drug is still active
Tolerance reduces the drug's effect over time
Sensitization weakens the response with use
Dependence is the same as tolerance

questions.explanation: Tolerance is the reduced response after repeated use. Withdrawal, sensitization and dependence are distinct phenomena.
questions.hint: The effect weakens with repeated use.

questions.stem: Why is reuptake an important way to end synaptic signalling?

answer.exemplar: Reuptake removes transmitter from the cleft back into the presynaptic neuron, stopping the signal and recycling the messenger for reuse.

questions.explanation: Reuptake clears the cleft and recycles transmitter. Without it signalling would linger and deplete stores.

questions.stem: Which ion movement restores the negative resting membrane potential after a spike?

options.text: Calcium entering restores the negative potential
Sodium leaving the cell restores the negative potential
Potassium leaving the cell restores the negative potential
Chloride leaving restores the negative potential

questions.explanation: Potassium efflux repolarizes the membrane. Sodium entry causes depolarization, not recovery.
questions.hint: The ion that exits to restore negativity.

questions.learningObjective: Map a lobe to auditory processing
questions.stem: A log places auditory processing in one of the four lobes. Which lobe is it, counting from the front?
questions.explanation: Counting from the front, the temporal lobe is the second lobe and handles auditory processing. The frontal is first, parietal third, occipital fourth.

questions.stem: A diagram highlights spatial attention as a right-hemisphere strength. Which option matches?

options.text: The right hemisphere has no specialized functions
The right hemisphere dominates language production
The right hemisphere controls fine motor speech
options.misconception: confuses speech motor with spatial attention

options.text: The right hemisphere excels at spatial attention

questions.explanation: The right hemisphere is stronger at spatial attention. Language production is usually left-lateralized.
questions.hint: Spatial attention is the right's strength.

questions.stem: Why does the hippocampus matter for turning short-term memories into long-term ones?

answer.exemplar: The hippocampus consolidates new declarative memories into durable cortical storage, so without it recent experiences fail to become lasting memories.

questions.explanation: The hippocampus binds and consolidates new memories for long-term storage. Without it recent experiences do not become lasting traces.

questions.stem: In Baddeley's model, which component directs attention and coordinates the slave systems?

options.text: The phonological loop directs attention and coordination
options.misconception: confuses a slave store with the controller

options.text: The central executive directs attention and coordination
The visuospatial sketchpad directs attention and coordination
options.misconception: confuses a slave store with the controller

options.text: The episodic buffer directs attention and coordination
options.misconception: confuses a slave store with the controller

questions.explanation: The central executive controls attention and coordinates the slave systems. The other components are storage buffers.

questions.stem: A log records a lesion of 2.5 cubic centimetres. If density is 1 gram per cubic centimetre, what is the mass in grams?
questions.explanation: Mass equals volume times density, so 2.5 cubic centimetres times 1 gram per cubic centimetre equals 2.5 grams. The value is unchanged by the unit density.

questions.stem: A sleep chart shows extra REM after a night of REM deprivation. What phenomenon is this?

options.text: Sleep inertia is extra REM after deprivation
Slow-wave rebound increases deep sleep after deprivation
REM rebound increases REM after deprivation
Circadian shift is extra REM after deprivation

questions.explanation: REM rebound is the increase in REM sleep after deprivation. The other terms describe different phenomena.
questions.hint: Extra REM after being deprived of it.

questions.stem: How can life experiences change gene expression without altering DNA sequence?

answer.exemplar: Epigenetic marks such as methylation switch genes on or off in response to experience, changing expression while the DNA sequence stays the same.

questions.explanation: Epigenetic mechanisms like methylation regulate gene expression without changing the DNA sequence. Experience can drive these marks.
questions.hint: Think marks that switch genes on or off.

questions.stem: What is the gap between two neurons across which chemical signals pass?

options.text: The soma is the gap between two neurons
options.misconception: confuses the cell body with a gap

options.text: The axon is the gap between two neurons
options.misconception: confuses a fibre with a gap

options.text: The dendrite is the gap between two neurons
options.misconception: confuses a branch with a gap

options.text: The synapse is the gap between two neurons

questions.explanation: The synapse is the junction or gap between neurons. Axons, dendrites and soma are parts of the cell, not the gap.

questions.stem: A log records a neuron firing at 50 hertz. How many spikes occur in 2 seconds?
questions.explanation: At 50 spikes per second, two seconds produce 100 spikes. Multiplying rate by time gives the count.

questions.stem: A diagram links a transmitter to muscle contraction and memory. Which transmitter is shown?

options.text: Dopamine activates muscles and supports memory
Acetylcholine activates muscles and supports memory
Serotonin activates muscles and supports memory
GABA activates muscles and supports memory

questions.explanation: Acetylcholine activates skeletal muscle and supports memory. The other transmitters have different primary roles.

questions.stem: Why does cerebellar damage produce clumsiness and poor balance?

answer.exemplar: The cerebellum fine-tunes movement timing and balance, so damage yields ataxia, tremor and unsteady gait.

questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates movement timing and balance. Damage disrupts fine motor control and produces ataxia.
